name: Bellari
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.note: Only classificatory notes (Andronov 2003, Bhat 1971) found; no descriptive phonology of Bellari located.

sources.citation: The Federal (Oct 2023). "Belare language dies with Sidda Belare: why languages never die alone" (news feature quoting Prof. A. Murigeppa).
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Reports that Belare has 11 vowel phonemes, 22 consonant phonemes and two diphthongs (per Murigeppa), names the CUK 2020 grammar, the villages of the community (Yedamoge, Eluru Karur, Alpadi, Mudur, Kalthodu, Aluru, Hosabalu, Rattadi, Amasebailu) and D.N.S. Bhat's earlier work; last fluent speaker Sidda Belare died 2023.

sources.citation: Bhat, D. N. Shankara. 1971. The Koraga language (Deccan College Linguistic Survey of India Series 7). Poona: Deccan College. Appendix 8, "The Belari language", pp. 119-123.
sources.note: Nothing. The 5-page Belari appendix gives a vocabulary list, Tulu p- > Belari h- and PDr *r > l correspondences, personal suffixes and a verb paradigm of bar 'come'; no phonology section and no mention of stress, accent, pitch or prominence. A a full-text search for stress/accent the whole book (including the three Koraga phonology sections) finds no 'stress' or 'accent' at all.

sources.citation: Andronov, M. S. 1970. Dravidian Languages. Moscow: Nauka.
sources.note: Does not mention Belari/Bellari at all (the only 'Bellari' is Bellary district in a list of Telugu dialect areas); pre-dates Bhat's discovery. Not a Bellari source.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page bell1261; English and Kannada Wikipedia 'Bellari language'.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Glottolog lists only Andronov 2003 (classification) and Bhat 1971; Wikipedia gives family placement, the 2023 extinction report and the Steever 1998 note that language-vs-Tulu-dialect status was uncertain.

sources.citation: Central University of Karnataka, Centre for Endangered Languages: other Belare documentation outputs (Kannada-language reports, recordings) from the Murigeppa/Harihara project on ten endangered speech forms of south India (Arebashe, Belare, Betta Kuruba, Beary, Chenchu, Erava, Havyaka, Koracha, Pattegar, Sankethi).

sources.note: The project that produced the 2020 grammar may have posted reports or audio; the CUK website is a JavaScript app that could not be reached by automated download for guessed Centre pages and could not be searched by automated download.

sources.citation: Murigeppa, A. & Mahendra Harihara. 2020. A grammar of Belare (Studies of Endangered Languages Series 03). Kalaburagi: Centre for Endangered Languages, Central University of Karnataka. xi+187 pp., with Belare-English-Kannada dictionary. LCCN 2022338638.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: The only full descriptive grammar of the language, based on fieldwork with the last speaker; the author reports a full phoneme inventory (11 V, 22 C, 2 diphthongs), so a phonology chapter exists and is the one place a Bellari stress statement is likely to be found. Not digitized (Library of Congress: digitized false; Google Books no preview). Copies: Library of Congress (PL4618.1 M87 2020, acquired via New Delhi office), Central University of Karnataka.

sources.citation: Andronov, Michail S. 2003. A Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian Languages. Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz. ISBN 3447044551.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Comparative grammar with a family-level section on accent that lists individual languages; it names Bellari in its morphology sections. Would at best give a second-hand, family-level stress statement, not a Bellari description. Google Books snippet view only (id vhB60gYvnLgC); search-inside could not be reached by automated download.
